lessons.name: Agile & parkour locomotion
lessons.summary: Agile locomotion coordinates sensing and rapid leg movements to jump gaps, climb obstacles, and land without falling.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Agile locomotion coordinates sensing and rapid leg movements to jump gaps, climb obstacles, and land without falling.

![Quadruped robot on the Extreme Parkour obstacle course](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-parkour.webp)
*Extreme Parkour policy demonstration. Source: [Extreme Parkour authors](https://extreme-parkour.github.io/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Walking is not enough:** gaps and high steps demand coordinated takeoff, flight, and landing rather than a faster version of flat-ground walking.
- **A concrete target:** Extreme Parkour reports jumping obstacles twice the robot's height and gaps twice its length; these are demonstrated results, not universal guarantees.
- **Start virtually:** the authors' browser demo lets us inspect obstacle crossings before attempting the linked project Replay a simulated jump with contact overlays.

> **Key idea:** The useful skill is choosing motion that fits the obstacle, not merely producing a spectacular jump.

## How it works

- **Look ahead:** a depth camera measures distance to visible surfaces, giving the controller information about approaching gaps, steps, and ramps.
- **Choose an action:** a neural-network **policy**, a function mapping observations to commands, repeatedly controls the robot rather than selecting a prerecorded animation.
- **Learn through attempts:** reinforcement learning rewards useful simulated behavior; the authors show that rewarding clearance helps avoid clipping gap edges.
- **Software analogy:** think of a game agent receiving a new observation each update, with physics determining whether its proposed action succeeds.
- **Worked comparison:** replay the authors' gap demonstration beside their no-clearance-reward failure; mark where each robot's feet first touch the far edge.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C["Depth image"] --> P["Policy"]
  P --> A["Leg commands"]
  A --> R["Robot and terrain"]
  R --> C
```

## Key terms

- **Depth image**: an image whose values describe distance rather than color.
- **Clearance**: space between the robot and an obstacle while crossing it.
- **Distillation**: training another policy to reproduce useful behavior; the repository separates base-policy and camera-policy training.
- **Generalization**: succeeding on obstacle arrangements or properties different from those used during training.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand contact changes and learned control; watch the failure examples before interpreting a successful course traversal.
- **After:** Build a held-out virtual parkour course becomes a meaningful test, with unseen obstacles rather than only replayed successes.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Open the browser demo** and identify a step, gap, and tilted ramp in the project videos.
2. **Annotate one crossing** with approach, takeoff, flight, and landing; note which feet support the body.
3. **Compare the failure clips** against successful crossings and write one testable explanation for an edge collision.
4. **Draft a benchmark table** listing obstacle type, completion, and contact mistakes; keep this first exercise entirely virtual.

lessons.name: Bipedal walking control
lessons.summary: Bipedal walking control coordinates body motion and alternating foot support so a two-legged robot can keep taking steps.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Bipedal walking control coordinates body motion and alternating foot support so a two-legged robot can keep taking steps.

![MIT diagram showing footstep and zero-moment-point planning for a walking robot](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-biped.webp)
*Footstep and body-motion planning. Source: [Russ Tedrake](https://underactuated.mit.edu/humanoids.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Two legs change the problem:** a lifted foot cannot support the body, so the controller must coordinate moving a leg with supporting its weight.
- **Begin with a small model:** MIT's walking notes separate footstep choice, body-motion planning, and whole-body motion instead of solving everything simultaneously.
- **A useful first project:** Reproduce preview-style flat-ground walking makes these decisions visible before dealing with a full humanoid such as Unitree G1.

> **Key idea:** Planning the body's motion and planning its supporting contacts are parts of the same walking problem.

## How it works

- **Select contacts:** choose where and when the feet will touch; a supporting foot pushes on the ground while the other leg swings forward.
- **Plan the body:** a simplified inverted pendulum treats the body as a mass above the ground, keeping its height constant.
- **Use pressure wisely:** on flat ground, the center of pressure stays inside the region spanned by supporting contacts.
- **Track and correct:** Drake's ZMP planner produces both a nominal body trajectory and feedback using measured body position and velocity.
- **Software analogy:** footsteps are a schedule of available workers; body control must finish its work without relying on a worker currently offline.
- **Worked toy example:** with height 1 m, body position 0.10 m, pressure point 0 m, and gravity 9.81 m/s², predicted forward acceleration is 0.981 m/s².

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  F["Footstep plan"] --> Z["Pressure-point plan"]
  Z --> B["Body trajectory"]
  B --> C["Feedback controller"]
  C --> R["Robot"]
  R --> C
```

## Key terms

- **Stance**: the part of a step when a foot supports the body.
- **Swing**: the part when a foot moves to its next contact.
- **Center of mass**: the position representing the body's mass distribution for translational motion.
- **Zero-moment point**: a point with zero horizontal tipping moment; on flat terrain it coincides with the center of pressure.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand forces and feedback; distinguish a body's position from its velocity before interpreting a walking trajectory.
- **After:** Reproduce preview-style flat-ground walking can test how changing footstep timing changes the required body motion.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Sketch two footprints** and a body point above them; label the currently supporting foot.
2. **Recompute the toy example** with the pressure point at 0.10 m, then 0.20 m; compare acceleration directions.
3. **Explore MIT's ZMP example** and change footstep timing as the chapter suggests.
4. **Record the assumptions:** flat ground and constant body height simplify the model; do not treat the sketch as a complete humanoid controller.

lessons.name: Central pattern generators
lessons.summary: Central pattern generators use interacting oscillators to produce rhythmic movement commands that can be adjusted by feedback.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Central pattern generators use interacting oscillators to produce rhythmic movement commands that can be adjusted by feedback.

![EPFL figure illustrating periodic patterns for programmable central pattern generators](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-cpg.webp)
*Periodic patterns for programmable CPGs. Source: [EPFL BioRob](https://www.epfl.ch/labs/biorob/page-36367-en-html/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Walking repeats:** a rhythm generator gives us an explicit way to describe repetition instead of hand-writing every joint target at every instant.
- **Inspect a compact controller:** frequency, amplitude, and relative timing are understandable knobs for a first locomotion experiment.
- **Connect code to movement:** Couple four gait oscillators is a useful first project because plots reveal coordination before a robot touches the floor.

> **Key idea:** A rhythm generator supplies movement structure; feedback and the body still determine whether that rhythm produces useful locomotion.

## How it works

- **Start with an oscillator:** a small dynamical system repeatedly changes state, like a clock hand going around a circle.
- **Couple several oscillators:** each oscillator influences others, helping preserve timing relationships between different movement signals.
- **Shape the output:** amplitude controls signal size and frequency controls repetition speed; a periodic pattern can become a movement command.
- **Software analogy:** imagine cooperating event loops sharing timing information, rather than independent timers drifting apart while each replays its own animation.
- **Learn the knobs:** CPG-RL trains a policy to modulate oscillator amplitude and frequency, combining an explicit rhythm with learned control.
- **Worked toy example:** plot two unit sine waves with a half-cycle offset; when one reaches its maximum, the other reaches its minimum.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  O["Coupled oscillators"] --> T["Movement targets"]
  T --> R["Robot"]
  R --> S["Sensory feedback"]
  S --> O
```

## Key terms

- **Phase**: position within a repeating cycle, like the angle of a clock hand.
- **Frequency**: how many complete cycles occur per unit time.
- **Amplitude**: the size of an oscillation around its center.
- **Coupling**: influence between oscillators that coordinates their timing.
- **Limit cycle**: a repeating trajectory in a system's state; stable ones attract nearby trajectories after small disturbances.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Know what a gait cycle represents and how a changing target differs from a motor's measured position.
- **After:** Couple four gait oscillators becomes the foundation for Add contact phase resets, where contact information changes rhythmic timing.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Plot two sine waves** across several cycles using the same frequency and a half-cycle offset.
2. **Change frequency alone** and observe shorter cycles without changing the range of values.
3. **Change amplitude alone** and observe larger signals without changing their repetition rate.
4. **Compare with CPG-RL:** identify which parameters are learned and which observations supply feedback; keep these first experiments as plots, not hardware commands.

lessons.name: Cross-embodiment locomotion policies
lessons.summary: Cross-embodiment locomotion policies reuse learned movement control across different robot bodies instead of training a separate controller for every robot.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Cross-embodiment locomotion policies reuse learned movement control across different robot bodies instead of training a separate controller for every robot.

![GenLoco published simulation montage showing different quadruped bodies](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-cross-embodiment.webp)
*Different quadruped bodies in GenLoco. Source: [GenLoco authors](https://github.com/HybridRobotics/GenLoco), Apache-2.0.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Bodies are not interchangeable:** robots can differ in proportions, joint conventions, and controller settings even when they all have four legs.
- **Reuse is the goal:** GenLoco studies whether training on procedurally varied simulated bodies produces controllers that transfer to unseen quadrupeds with similar structures.
- **A bounded example:** its repository demonstrates pacing and spinning across ten robots, using one policy for each motion, not one universal controller for every skill.

> **Key idea:** Reusing policy weights does not remove the need to define and test each robot's control interface.

## How it works

- **Vary the training bodies:** morphology randomization changes simulated robot bodies so the controller cannot rely exclusively on one robot's proportions.
- **Learn shared behavior:** a policy maps its inputs to movement commands while training imitates reference motions.
- **Adapt the interface:** GenLoco's new-robot instructions require a robot description, joint ordering, motor directions, initial angles, and suitable feedback gains.
- **Test unseen bodies:** evaluate the same trained policy on another body rather than retraining it and calling that transfer.
- **Software analogy:** shared policy weights resemble reusable business logic; each robot still needs an adapter with correctly ordered arguments and meaningful units.
- **Worked interface example:** GenLoco's A1 configuration lists four legs with three motors each: twelve motor entries whose ordering must remain consistent.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M["Varied simulated bodies"] --> T["Train shared policy"]
  T --> P["Frozen policy"]
  O["New body observations"] --> P
  P --> A["Robot-specific interface"]
  A --> R["New robot"]
  R --> O
```

## Key terms

- **Embodiment**: the physical body through which a controller senses and acts.
- **Morphology**: the body's structure and proportions.
- **Zero-shot transfer**: applying a trained controller to a new target without additional training there.
- **Policy**: a function selecting actions from its inputs.
- **Reference motion**: an example movement used as a training target.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand learned locomotion and joint control; distinguish changing a robot configuration from changing a policy's learned weights.
- **After:** Test one policy on scaled virtual quadrupeds can separate interface mistakes from genuine limits of body-to-body transfer.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Watch the GenLoco demonstration** and list which bodies share a pacing controller.
2. **Inspect the A1 configuration** and locate motor names, motor directions, and the twelve initial joint angles.
3. **Read Adding New Robots** and make a checklist of adapter fields required for a second body.
4. **Design a comparison:** keep policy weights fixed, vary the simulated body, and record falls and motion tracking; do not assume transfer beyond tested structures.

lessons.name: Fall recovery & get-up
lessons.summary: Fall recovery uses coordinated contacts and joint movements to bring a fallen robot back to a stable standing posture.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Fall recovery uses coordinated contacts and joint movements to bring a fallen robot back to a stable standing posture.

![VIGOR diagram showing human recovery demonstrations, robot poses, terrain alignment, and a recovery controller](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-recovery.webp)
*VIGOR learns terrain-aware fall recovery. Source: [VIGOR authors](https://vigor2026.github.io/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A fall is not a reset:** a physical robot remains on the floor until something moves it; walking control alone does not solve this.
- **Start with evidence:** the ANYmal study demonstrates learned recovery from complex fallen configurations after training in simulation.
- **Terrain changes the task:** VIGOR studies humanoid recovery around stairs, gaps, and other non-flat surfaces, not merely standing up on an empty floor.

> **Key idea:** Successful recovery means regaining usable support, not briefly passing through an upright-looking pose.

## How it works

- **Observe the starting state:** joint positions and body orientation describe how the robot is folded; depth sensing can reveal surrounding surfaces.
- **Choose a recovery action:** a learned **policy**, a function mapping observations to commands, coordinates joints to change body pose and supporting contacts.
- **Account for the ground:** VIGOR combines demonstrations of recovery movements with varied simulated terrain, then trains a controller using depth and internal sensing.
- **Separate the stages:** impact mitigation reduces damage during a fall; get-up control moves an already fallen robot toward standing.
- **Software analogy:** a database recovery procedure restores invariants before accepting requests; likewise, our walking supervisor should check support before resuming velocity commands.
- **Worked example:** VIGOR activates its controller after a 20° tilt in fall tests; this is an experimental trigger, not a universal safe threshold.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S["Pose and terrain"] --> P["Recovery policy"]
  P --> A["Joint commands"]
  A --> C["Changing contacts"]
  C --> S
```

## Key terms

- **Proprioception**: measurements of the robot's own state, such as joint positions, rather than an external view.
- **Support contact**: a body part touching a surface and carrying load during movement.
- **Impact mitigation**: reducing harmful contact effects while falling.
- **Stand-up recovery**: coordinated motion from a fallen configuration toward standing.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Know joint limits and contact forces; classify a fallen pose separately from a temporary walking disturbance.
- **After:** The project **Catalogue simulated fallen poses** supplies test cases for the project **Train or replay a simulated get-up controller**.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Watch the ANYmal video** and label back-down, side-down, and tangled-leg starting configurations where visible.
2. **Inspect VIGOR's stand-up examples** and list surfaces that can support or obstruct a recovering limb.
3. **Build a test table** with initial pose, terrain, final support, and whether the robot remains standing.
4. **Specify a handover check** for the project **Switch safely between walking and recovery**; keep this first exercise in simulation or video analysis.

lessons.name: Gaits & gait cycles
lessons.summary: A gait specifies when each foot supports the robot and when it swings toward its next contact.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

A gait specifies when each foot supports the robot and when it swings toward its next contact.

![Stanford Pupper controller diagram routing each leg between stance and swing according to a gait scheduler](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-gaits.webp)
*Pupper separates contact scheduling from foot movement. Source: [Stanford Robotics Club](https://github.com/stanfordroboticsclub/StanfordQuadruped), MIT.*

## Why it matters for us

- **One body, different rhythms:** a quadruped can move its diagonal legs together in a trot instead of moving every leg independently.
- **Timing comes before angles:** a gait scheduler decides which feet should support the body; other controllers decide how those feet move.
- **Make coordination visible:** the project **Build an interactive gait phase viewer** turns an invisible timing schedule into something we can inspect and debug.

> **Key idea:** A gait is a contact schedule, not proof that the robot can physically execute it without slipping or falling.

## How it works

- **Repeat a cycle:** track progress through one repeating sequence, then wrap around to its beginning.
- **Assign foot roles:** a stance foot stays on the ground while the body moves; a swing foot lifts and returns toward its next touchdown.
- **Coordinate pairs:** Pupper's trot moves diagonal pairs together, with intervals when all four feet are scheduled to remain in contact.
- **Software analogy:** Pupper uses a modulo counter, like indexing a circular buffer; a lookup table converts the current phase into four contact flags.
- **Worked timing example:** its configuration uses 0.10 s overlap, 0.15 s swing, then repeats those durations: one cycle lasts 0.50 s.
- **Derive the support fraction:** each leg's configured stance lasts 0.35 s, so its duty factor is 0.35 / 0.50 = 0.70.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  T["Tick counter"] --> P["Cycle phase"]
  P --> F["Contact flags"]
  F --> S["Stance or swing"]
  S --> J["Joint targets"]
```

## Key terms

- **Stance**: the interval when a foot supports the robot.
- **Swing**: the interval when a foot travels to its next contact.
- **Phase**: progress through a repeating movement cycle.
- **Duty factor**: the fraction of a cycle that a foot spends in stance.
- **Touchdown**: the transition from swing to ground contact.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand time-based loops and a foot's position relative to the body; distinguish a planned contact from a measured one.
- **After:** The project **Compare gait energy and slip** asks whether an attractive timing pattern also produces useful physical movement.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Read Pupper's contact table** and draw four horizontal timelines, one per leg.
2. **Mark the four phases** using the configured overlap and swing durations; check the total against 0.50 s.
3. **Implement a modulo counter** and display the four contact flags across two cycles.
4. **Compare with the video:** identify diagonal pairing, then explain which parts of foot movement the contact flags do not specify.

lessons.name: Humanoid motion imitation & retargeting
lessons.summary: Retargeting maps human movement onto a robot's body, while motion imitation trains a controller to perform that movement under physical constraints.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Retargeting maps human movement onto a robot's body, while motion imitation trains a controller to perform that movement under physical constraints.

![ASAP pipeline mapping human videos to humanoid imitation goals, simulation training, and real-world motion](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-retargeting.webp)
*ASAP separates motion goals, tracking policies, and physics alignment. Source: [ASAP authors](https://agile.human2humanoid.com/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Human joints are not robot joints:** a captured dance cannot simply become an array of motor commands for a differently proportioned humanoid.
- **References express intent:** motion data tells a controller what movement to reproduce; physics still determines whether the robot stays supported.
- **A visible learning goal:** the project **Retarget your own dance to a humanoid** exposes the difference between matching a pose and executing a motion.

> **Key idea:** Retargeting supplies a movement target; a tracking controller must make that target work on the robot.

## How it works

- **Describe the example:** a motion clip records a sequence of body poses rather than a single image.
- **Map between bodies:** retargeting converts that sequence into robot movement goals despite differences in structure and proportions.
- **Train a tracker:** DeepMimic combines a motion-imitation objective with task goals in physical simulation; it is foundational character-control research, not automatic hardware deployment.
- **Address deployment mismatch:** ASAP first trains tracking policies using retargeted human motion, then uses real trajectories to learn a correction model inside the simulator.
- **Software analogy:** a compiler translates source into another machine's representation; retargeting is translation, while physical tracking resembles executing and testing the compiled program.
- **Worked pipeline example:** ASAP evaluates three transfers: IsaacGym to IsaacSim, IsaacGym to Genesis, and IsaacGym to a real Unitree G1.
- **Keep the correction separate:** ASAP fine-tunes with its correction model inside simulation, then deploys the improved policy without that model.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  H["Human motion"] --> R["Retarget"]
  R --> G["Robot motion goals"]
  G --> T["Train tracker"]
  T --> P["Tracking policy"]
  P --> B["Robot movement"]
```

## Key terms

- **Pose**: the positions and orientations describing the body at one instant.
- **Retargeting**: adapting motion goals from one body structure to another.
- **Tracking error**: the difference between desired movement and movement actually achieved.
- **Dynamics mismatch**: differences between simulated and real physical responses.
- **Residual model**: a model of a correction to another model or command.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand joint coordinates, physical contacts, and learned control; separate an example trajectory from a controller.
- **After:** The project **Compare nominal and residual-dynamics tracking** tests whether physics alignment improves execution rather than only making a reference animation look better.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Watch the ASAP comparisons** and choose one movement with clear support changes.
2. **Annotate the motion pipeline** with human poses, robot reference poses, and executed poses as three separate outputs.
3. **Inspect the before/after clips** and describe one visible tracking difference without claiming a numerical improvement.
4. **Write a retargeting checklist** covering body proportions, joint limits, and foot contacts before planning a simulation-only dance experiment.

lessons.name: Leg design & proprioceptive actuation
lessons.summary: Leg geometry and transmission design determine how joint motors move the feet, deliver forces, and respond when the feet hit the ground.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Leg geometry and transmission design determine how joint motors move the feet, deliver forces, and respond when the feet hit the ground.

![MIT Cheetah's custom motors and amplifier electronics](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-leg-design.webp)
*Custom high-torque-density motors and amplifier for MIT Cheetah. Source: [Jose-Luis Olivares/MIT](https://news.mit.edu/2014/mit-cheetah-robot-runs-jumps-0915), Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives.*

## Why it matters for us

- **A leg is a transmission:** changing link lengths or gearing changes what motor movement means at the foot, even with identical control software.
- **Ground contact is unavoidable:** a walking leg must swing freely, support weight, and tolerate repeated collisions with the floor.
- **Design before purchasing:** the project **Plot a leg workspace and force map** helps us compare mechanical choices before building a complete quadruped.

> **Key idea:** Select leg geometry and actuation together; accurate joint positioning alone does not guarantee controllable ground forces.

## How it works

- **Choose the geometry:** link lengths and joint arrangements determine where the foot can reach.
- **Choose the transmission:** a gearbox trades motor speed against output torque, the twisting effort applied around a joint.
- **Limit reflected inertia:** high reduction can make the motor's inertia harder to accelerate from the joint side, affecting impact response.
- **Allow backdriving:** an external foot force can move the joints and motor rather than meeting an almost rigid transmission.
- **Control interaction internally:** MIT's proprioceptive approach controls foot interaction through joint-level torque control, using low-ratio transmission and low-inertia legs.
- **Software analogy:** choosing storage by throughput alone ignores latency; choosing an actuator by peak torque alone ignores how quickly and gently it can respond to contact.
- **Worked design example:** the MIT Cheetah study reports controlled ground contacts as short as 85 ms with peak forces exceeding 450 N.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  C["Joint torque command"] --> M["Motor and transmission"]
  M --> L["Leg geometry"]
  L --> F["Foot interaction"]
  F --> J["Joint response"]
  J --> C
```

## Key terms

- **Workspace**: the set of foot positions reachable with the chosen leg geometry.
- **Torque**: rotational effort around a joint.
- **Gear reduction**: a transmission ratio that reduces speed while increasing available output torque, subject to losses.
- **Backdrivability**: how readily external load motion can drive the transmission backward.
- **Proprioceptive actuation**: controlling interaction through sensing and control local to the robot's actuators rather than relying on foot-force feedback.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand linkage motion and joint torque; distinguish a position-controlled servo from a force-control-oriented actuator design.
- **After:** The project **Compare virtual leg ratios** can evaluate reach and interaction trade-offs, not simply whether a leg animation looks plausible.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Inspect the motor photo** and locate the actuator as a separate component from the leg links.
2. **Sketch two leg geometries** and mark which foot positions each can reach.
3. **Read the paper's actuator comparison** and label high-ratio gearing, a series spring, and proprioceptive actuation.
4. **Make a comparison table** for reach, impact response, and sensing needs; keep this first study virtual rather than testing impacts on hardware.

lessons.name: Loco-manipulation coordination
lessons.summary: Loco-manipulation coordinates stepping, body posture, and object interaction so the robot can move and manipulate without treating balance as a separate problem.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Loco-manipulation coordinates stepping, body posture, and object interaction so the robot can move and manipulate without treating balance as a separate problem.

![RoboDuet quadruped robots with arms in different coordinated body and arm configurations](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-loco-manipulation.webp)
*RoboDuet coordinates an arm with a legged body. Source: [RoboDuet authors](https://locomanip-duet.github.io/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **The arm moves the problem:** reaching with an arm changes the whole robot's configuration, so a fixed walking posture can unnecessarily restrict useful reach.
- **Objects push back:** contact-rich manipulation requires reasoning about force as well as the hand's position.
- **Start with a controlled task:** the project **Step while pushing a known object** isolates coordination without also requiring general object recognition.

> **Key idea:** The hand's task and the feet's supporting role must agree on what the whole body should do.

## How it works

- **Specify the interaction:** provide a desired hand position and orientation; some methods also accept force commands for contact with objects.
- **Coordinate body and arm:** RoboDuet uses cooperating locomotion and arm policies rather than treating the arm as an independent passenger.
- **Share useful commands:** its arm policy adjusts body-orientation commands while controlling the arm joints, allowing body posture to assist reaching.
- **Handle contact forces:** position-and-force-control research estimates interaction forces from state history and compensates through position and velocity adjustments.
- **Software analogy:** two services updating one shared record need a coordination protocol; independently valid arm and walking commands can still conflict over the body's posture.
- **Worked task example:** RoboDuet demonstrates object transport at ground, chair, cabinet, and desk levels: 0, 20, 60, and 100 cm in its setup.
- **Distinguish evidence from scope:** these demonstrations show coordinated tasks, not a guarantee of success with arbitrary objects, payloads, or surfaces.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G["Hand goal"] --> A["Arm policy"]
  A --> L["Locomotion policy"]
  A --> J["Arm commands"]
  L --> F["Leg commands"]
  J --> R["Robot and object"]
  F --> R
  R --> A
  R --> L
```

## Key terms

- **End effector**: the working tool at the arm's tip, such as a gripper.
- **Pose tracking**: following a requested position and orientation over time.
- **Whole-body coordination**: choosing limb and body actions together to accomplish a task.
- **Interaction force**: a force exchanged between the robot and an object or surface.
- **Compliance**: allowing motion in response to contact rather than rigidly opposing every displacement.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand supporting contacts and body balance; separate a hand target from the body motion needed to achieve it.
- **After:** The project **Walk with a moving virtual payload** can test coordination, while the project **Step while pushing a known object** adds external interaction.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Watch RoboDuet's door-opening clip** and identify arm motion, body-posture changes, and steps as separate observations.
2. **Compare its transport demonstrations** at the four published heights; note when arm motion alone would be insufficient.
3. **Sketch a pushing test** with one known object and one requested hand trajectory, entirely in simulation.
4. **Define evaluation columns** for hand error, object movement, and falls; a successful hand trajectory alone is not enough.

lessons.name: Model predictive control for legged robots
lessons.summary: Model predictive control repeatedly predicts a short future, optimizes feasible robot actions, and updates the plan using fresh measurements.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Model predictive control repeatedly predicts a short future, optimizes feasible robot actions, and updates the plan using fresh measurements.

![OCS2 legged-robot MPC example visualized with a quadruped and supporting feet](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-mpc.webp)
*A frame from OCS2's legged-robot example. Source: [OCS2 contributors](https://leggedrobotics.github.io/ocs2/robotic_examples.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Look beyond the current error:** pushing harder now can help or hurt the robot's posture several steps later.
- **Respect physical limits:** a lifted foot cannot push the ground, and a supporting foot cannot supply unlimited sideways force without slipping.
- **An inspectable starting point:** the project **Inspect a contact-force MPC rollout** lets us study predicted movement before trying hardware.

> **Key idea:** Optimize a future sequence, use its immediate action, then replan rather than blindly executing the entire prediction.

## How it works

- **Estimate the state:** describe the body's position, orientation, and motion using current measurements.
- **Predict the response:** a dynamics model estimates how candidate foot forces will move the robot over a finite future interval.
- **Score candidate plans:** an objective penalizes unwanted motion or large commands; constraints exclude actions that violate the model's contact rules.
- **Software analogy:** a scheduler repeatedly replans queued work after receiving new load measurements; the predicted queue is useful, but not an irrevocable script.
- **Simplify for speed:** the Cheetah 3 study optimizes ground forces using simplified body dynamics, rather than simulating every joint inside its optimizer.
- **Keep contact choices explicit:** OCS2's quadruped example receives a user-defined gait; swing feet have zero force and stance feet have zero velocity.
- **Worked timing example:** the Cheetah paper reports horizons up to 0.5 s and updates at 20–30 Hz: roughly 10–15 update intervals fit inside that horizon.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S["Measured state"] --> P["Predict future motion"]
  P --> O["Optimize constrained actions"]
  O --> A["Apply immediate action"]
  A --> R["Robot moves"]
  R --> S
```

## Key terms

- **Prediction horizon**: the future time interval considered during one optimization.
- **Objective**: a numerical score that the optimizer tries to reduce.
- **Constraint**: a rule the planned states or actions must satisfy.
- **Ground reaction force**: the force the ground applies to a contacting foot.
- **Convex optimization**: a problem structure that avoids competing local minima and supports efficient solvers.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand forces, feedback, and constrained optimization; distinguish a contact schedule from the forces applied during each scheduled contact.
- **After:** The project **Reproduce a simulated MPC trot** turns predictions into motion; **Compare convex and nonlinear contact control** is the subsequent comparison project.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Watch the Cheetah video** and identify which feet are supporting the body during one short sequence.
2. **Inspect OCS2's legged example** and list its swing-foot, stance-foot, and friction constraints.
3. **Draw a 0.5 s prediction** with 20 Hz replanning marks; distinguish each new plan from the original prediction.
4. **Design a rollout log** with desired motion, predicted body motion, contact forces, and constraint violations; reserve hardware deployment for later.

lessons.name: Multirotor flight dynamics & control
lessons.summary: A multirotor controls flight by changing rotor thrusts, using nested feedback loops to turn position goals into body rotation and motor commands.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

A multirotor controls flight by changing rotor thrusts, using nested feedback loops to turn position goals into body rotation and motor commands.

![PX4 diagram showing position, velocity, angle, angular-rate controllers and motor mixing](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-multirotor.webp)
*PX4's published multicopter cascade; implementation rates vary by platform. Source: [PX4 contributors](https://docs.px4.io/main/en/flight_stack/controller_diagrams.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Translation needs rotation:** a conventional quadcopter tilts its thrust direction to accelerate sideways; moving horizontally is not a separate wheel-like command.
- **Stabilization is continuous:** the controller must correct orientation disturbances while pursuing a position goal.
- **A useful first experiment:** the project **Animate thrust and attitude coupling** shows why keeping altitude becomes harder when the vehicle tilts.

> **Key idea:** The outer loop requests motion; the inner loops make the vehicle point and rotate appropriately to produce it.

## How it works

- **Generate force and torque:** rotor thrusts add to move the body; differences between rotor outputs also turn it.
- **Track position:** PX4's position controller requests velocity, and its velocity controller requests acceleration.
- **Choose thrust direction:** requested acceleration becomes a thrust magnitude and an attitude, meaning the body's orientation.
- **Stabilize rotation:** an attitude loop requests angular rate; the rate loop corrects how fast the body is rotating.
- **Software analogy:** a high-level API requests a destination while lower-level handlers translate it into concrete operations; motor allocation is the hardware-specific backend.
- **Allocate motor commands:** PX4 translates desired thrust and torque into actuator outputs using the airframe's geometry, rather than embedding every motor layout in the controller.
- **Worked timing example:** Bitcraze documents 500 Hz attitude/rate loops and 100 Hz position/velocity loops for its cascaded PID: five inner updates per outer update.
- **Read rates carefully:** the PX4 figure illustrates another configuration; do not copy its rates into a Crazyflie tuning exercise.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  P["Position goal"] --> V["Velocity goal"]
  V --> A["Thrust and attitude"]
  A --> R["Angular-rate goal"]
  R --> M["Motor allocation"]
  M --> D["Drone and sensing"]
  D --> P
```

## Key terms

- **Thrust**: the propeller-generated force that accelerates the vehicle.
- **Attitude**: the body's orientation, often described as roll, pitch, and yaw.
- **Angular rate**: how quickly orientation changes around an axis.
- **Setpoint**: a desired value supplied to a feedback controller.
- **Cascade**: nested controllers where one loop supplies the next loop's setpoint.
- **Control allocation**: translating desired body forces and torques into individual actuator commands.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand proportional, integral, and derivative feedback, plus the difference between a rotation angle and its rate of change.
- **After:** The project **Tune a simulated hover cascade** provides a safer precursor to the project **Fly a Crazyflie with the stock cascaded PID**.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Watch the hover explanation** and trace a position request down to motor commands.
2. **Label each PX4 block** with its input and output units: position, velocity, acceleration, angle, rate, or actuator command.
3. **Draw Bitcraze's update timeline** with five 2 ms inner ticks per 10 ms outer tick.
4. **Plan a simulated disturbance test** and plot orientation and position separately; keep real propellers out of this first experiment.

lessons.name: Perceptive rough-terrain locomotion
lessons.summary: Perceptive locomotion uses observations of upcoming ground to adapt movement before contact, while retaining feedback from the robot's own body.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Perceptive locomotion uses observations of upcoming ground to adapt movement before contact, while retaining feedback from the robot's own body.

![ANYmal terrain-height maps compared with real stairs, snow, vegetation, reflective ground, and sensor occlusion](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-rough-terrain.webp)
*Terrain maps can be incomplete or misleading even when the robot can walk there. Source: [Takahiro Miki and collaborators](https://leggedrobotics.github.io/rl-perceptiveloco/), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **See before stepping:** sensing upcoming stairs or uneven ground lets a robot adapt earlier than waiting for a foot to collide.
- **Appearance can mislead:** vegetation, snow, and reflective surfaces can make measured terrain differ from the surface that actually supports a foot.
- **Make the input visible:** the project **Render terrain-height foothold overlays** helps us inspect what a controller believes lies beneath its next steps.

> **Key idea:** Terrain observations are evidence to combine with body feedback, not a perfect map that the feet must blindly obey.

## How it works

- **Observe the surroundings:** depth measurements describe distances to visible surfaces outside the robot.
- **Build a usable representation:** the ETH perceptive-locomotion system samples heights from an elevation map built using measured 3D points.
- **Combine internal sensing:** joint and body measurements provide information about actual movement and contact responses.
- **Software analogy:** a cached database read can be missing or stale; a controller should not treat a delayed terrain sample as unquestionable current state.
- **Remember uncertain evidence:** ETH's learned recurrent encoder combines external observations and internal sensing while retaining information across time.
- **Learn robustness deliberately:** its training includes noisy observations, with a simulated teacher providing targets for a controller that can run on the robot.
- **Worked field example:** the reported hiking route covered 2.2 km with 120 m elevation gain; completion took 78 minutes in that particular evaluation.
- **Recognize alternate inputs:** Extreme Parkour instead demonstrates a learned policy using a front-facing depth camera directly, without requiring this same elevation-map pipeline.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  T["Depth observations"] --> E["Terrain representation"]
  E --> F["Combine with body sensing"]
  B["Joint and body state"] --> F
  F --> C["Movement controller"]
  C --> R["Robot and ground"]
  R --> B
  R --> T
```

## Key terms

- **Exteroception**: sensing the environment outside the robot.
- **Proprioception**: sensing the robot's own configuration and movement.
- **Elevation map**: a representation assigning ground-height estimates to horizontal locations.
- **Occlusion**: something blocking a sensor's view of a surface.
- **Recurrent encoder**: a learned observation-processing component that carries information forward over time.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand stance and swing, feedback, and depth measurements; distinguish observed surface geometry from reliable support.
- **After:** The project **Compare blind and terrain-aware walking** isolates perception's contribution; the project **Inject depth delay into rough-terrain walking** tests stale inputs.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Inspect the terrain-map figure** and label missing observations separately from misleading height estimates.
2. **Watch the ETH examples** and compare visible terrain with the support the robot actually uses.
3. **Sketch a simulated comparison** using identical terrain and commands with and without terrain observations.
4. **Add delayed observations** to the test plan; record falls, completion, and foot collisions rather than judging only a successful-looking clip.

lessons.name: Reduced-order locomotion models
lessons.summary: Reduced-order models replace a many-jointed robot with a few variables, preserving selected walking or hopping dynamics while deliberately omitting other details.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Reduced-order models replace a many-jointed robot with a few variables, preserving selected walking or hopping dynamics while deliberately omitting other details.

![Spring-loaded inverted pendulum diagram with a point mass, spring leg, ground contact, leg length and angle](/img/lessons/knowledge_locomotion-reduced-models.webp)
*The spring-loaded inverted pendulum replaces a complete legged body with a mass and spring. Source: [Russ Tedrake](https://underactuated.mit.edu/simple_legs.html), license unknown.*

## Why it matters for us

- **Reason before simulating everything:** a small model exposes why a body accelerates or bounces without burying us in dozens of joint coordinates.
- **Pick the behavior to preserve:** nearly constant-height walking and springy running need different simplifications.
- **Build a controlled comparison:** the project **Simulate LIPM versus SLIP** lets us discover what each abstraction predicts and what it cannot represent.

> **Key idea:** A useful simplified model preserves the dynamics relevant to a question, not every detail of the robot's appearance.

## How it works

- **Gather the mass:** represent the robot through its center of mass, the point describing the average location of its mass.
- **Approximate walking:** a linear inverted pendulum model (LIPM) keeps that point at constant height and relates horizontal acceleration to its offset from support.
- **Approximate bouncing:** a spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) places a point mass above a massless spring leg.
- **Software analogy:** an interface mock reproduces selected behavior without implementing every dependency; a reduced model must similarly state which physical behavior its simplifications preserve.
- **Switch equations with contact:** SLIP uses free-flight motion in the air and spring-leg motion while its foot is anchored.
- **Worked state example:** SLIP's flight state has four values: horizontal position, height, and their two velocities; stance instead uses leg length, angle, and their rates.
- **Keep the omissions visible:** SLIP assumes its massless leg can reposition instantly in flight; a real actuator cannot meet that assumption exactly.
- **Choose richer abstractions when needed:** OCS2's single-rigid-body model includes orientation, while its centroidal model also incorporates limb motion into whole-body momentum.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  F["SLIP flight equations"] --> T["Touchdown"]
  T --> S["Spring-leg stance equations"]
  S --> L["Liftoff"]
  L --> F
```

## Key terms

- **Reduced order**: using fewer state variables than a detailed physical model.
- **State**: the variables needed to predict the model's next evolution.
- **LIPM**: a constant-height inverted-pendulum approximation for walking dynamics.
- **SLIP**: a point-mass and spring-leg approximation for bouncing locomotion.
- **Hybrid dynamics**: continuous motion combined with discrete changes, such as touchdown switching the governing equations.

## Before / after

- **Before:** Understand position, velocity, acceleration, and numerical integration; separate the model's state variables from a robot's complete joint configuration.
- **After:** The project **Map stable hopping parameters** explores the model; the project **Test reduced-model predictions on a full robot** probes its limitations.

## Try it in an afternoon

1. **Watch the LegLab examples** and identify flight, touchdown, stance, and liftoff in a hopping sequence.
2. **Inspect the SLIP figure** and list which real robot components have disappeared.
3. **Write two state records** with the four flight variables and four stance variables; label their units.
4. **Trace one hop's transitions** using touchdown and spring rest length as events, then list real-world effects missing from that model.
